groups.high: High-temperature short-time (HTST) pasteurization of ordinary milk uses at least 72°C (161°F) for 15 seconds, or an approved equivalent treatment. The FDA Pasteurized Milk Ordinance and Codex CXC 57-2004 provide the relevant process framework; some higher-fat, higher-solids, or sweetened products require higher temperatures. The objective is pathogen reduction, including Salmonella and E. coli O157:H7, while retaining acceptable product quality. Coxiella burnetii is an important heat-resistance benchmark. Pasteurization is not sterilization or commercial sterilization: bacterial spores and some heat-tolerant organisms can survive. It therefore does not make subsequent refrigeration unnecessary. An HTST plant must deliver the required temperature and holding time to every particle, not merely achieve a satisfactory average temperature. Heat exchangers, controlled flow, temperature recording, and diversion of inadequately heated milk help maintain that requirement. Process verification can include the alkaline phosphatase test, alongside equipment checks and records. Spore strips designed for sterilization are not a general substitute for milk-pasteurization validation. Avoid contamination after heating and maintain the cold chain. UHT processing uses a different, more severe treatment, generally combined with aseptic packaging for shelf-stable products. Neither an invented organism-specific log-reduction target nor a sterilization F0 calculation should be presented as the universal 72°C/15-second milk standard.
groups.mid: For ordinary milk, high-temperature short-time pasteurization, or HTST, means heating it to at least 72°C (161°F) for 15 seconds. An approved equivalent process can also be used when it delivers the required reduction in harmful germs. The FDA Pasteurized Milk Ordinance and Codex CXC 57-2004 set out the process rules. Milk products with more fat, more solids, or added sugar can need more heat. The objective is to reduce harmful organisms, including Salmonella and E. coli O157:H7, while preserving the milk's quality and nutritional value. A germ called Coxiella burnetii helps set the heat standard. Pasteurization does not make milk sterile. Some spores and heat-tolerant germs can live through it, so the milk still needs a cold chain. Every part of the milk must get enough heat for enough time. A good average reading is not enough. Plants use heat exchangers, flow controls, heat records, and a system that sends milk back if it is not hot enough. Checks can include an alkaline phosphatase test. This detects an enzyme that adequate pasteurization should inactivate, helping staff identify a potentially inadequate process. Staff also check the equipment and records. Spore strips used to check sterilizers do not replace these milk checks. Keep germs out after heating and keep the milk cold. UHT uses much more heat and usually clean, sealed packing to make a different, shelf-stable product. The 72°C rule does not by itself promise an exact fixed drop in each named germ.
groups.low: Milk needs heat to kill harmful germs. For ordinary milk, one method is HTST. It means using high heat for a short time to make milk safer. Heat all the milk to at least 72°C (161°F). Keep it there for at least 15 seconds. A different approved method may work too. The FDA milk rules and Codex CXC 57-2004 explain this. Milk with more fat, more solids, or added sugar may need more heat. The heat reduces harmful bacteria, such as Salmonella and E. coli O157:H7, that can cause foodborne illness. A germ called Coxiella burnetii helps set the heat rule. But the milk is not free of all germs. Some bacterial spores can survive the process, so keep the milk cold after this step. Do not let new germs get in. In a plant, each part of the milk must get enough heat. One good average is not enough. Staff check heat, flow, time, and records. Milk that is not hot enough goes back. One check is called the alkaline phosphatase test. It looks for an enzyme left in the milk. Staff also check that the equipment works correctly and that records show each batch met the standard. Spore strips for a sterilizer do not replace these checks. UHT milk gets much more heat. It is usually put in a clean, sealed pack. That is a different process. The HTST rule does not give one fixed kill rate for each germ.
groups.source_review: FDA PMO temperature table and FDA pathogen explanation checked; technical corrections made, not a plant-specific validation protocol.
groups.notes: Corrected 164°F to161°F; removed invented Salmonella/E.coli log targets, F0 equivalence, commercial sterility claim and spore-strip validation.

groups.high: Food-allergen labeling identifies ingredients that can trigger potentially life-threatening reactions. EU Regulation 1169/2011, Annex II, lists 14 groups: cereals containing gluten; crustaceans; eggs; fish; peanuts; soybeans; milk; specified tree nuts; celery; mustard; sesame; sulphur dioxide and sulphites above 10 mg/kg or 10 mg/L, expressed as total SO2; lupin; and molluscs. Listed exemptions apply to some derivatives. In prepacked foods, required allergen information is normally emphasized within the ingredient list. The United States recognizes nine major allergens: milk, eggs, fish, crustacean shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soybeans, and sesame. FALCPA established the original eight; the FASTER Act added sesame, effective January 1, 2023. Relevant FDA-regulated packaged foods must name the allergen source in the ingredients or an adjacent Contains statement. A technical ingredient name alone, such as casein, does not replace identifying milk. The US major-allergen list does not include every food capable of causing an allergy; the EU list is broader in several respects. Ingredient declarations must be distinguished from precautionary cross-contact warnings. In the US, May contain warnings are voluntary and cannot replace preventive controls or good manufacturing practice. There is no general EU rule requiring that exact warning whenever any detectable trace exists. Sulphite thresholds, exemptions, and applicable national rules matter. Check the full label each time, including when traveling, because formulations and jurisdictional requirements differ. Undeclared allergens can prompt recalls and other enforcement action.
groups.mid: Allergen labels help you avoid food that could cause a serious reaction. The EU uses Regulation 1169/2011, Annex II. It covers 14 groups: cereals with gluten; crustaceans; eggs; fish; peanuts; soybeans; milk; listed tree nuts; celery; mustard; sesame; sulphur dioxide and sulphites; lupin; and molluscs. For sulphites, the rule applies above 10 mg/kg or 10 mg/L as total SO2. Certain processed derivatives have specific statutory exemptions, so the applicable ingredient and jurisdiction must be checked. On prepacked foods, allergens usually stand out in the ingredients list, such as in bold type. The US has nine major allergens: milk, eggs, fish, crustacean shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soybeans, and sesame. FALCPA first covered eight. The FASTER Act added sesame from January 1, 2023. On relevant FDA-regulated packs, the allergen source must be named in the ingredients or a nearby Contains statement. Casein, for example, must be linked to milk; the technical name alone is not enough. These lists do not include every food that can cause an allergy. EU and US rules also differ. A listed ingredient is not the same as a May contain warning. In the US, these cross-contact warnings are voluntary. They do not replace good factory practice or controls that keep allergens out. The EU does not have one general rule that every trace needs that exact warning. Thresholds and exemptions still matter. Check the whole label each time, even on a familiar food. Recipes may change, and a label abroad may follow different rules. Missing allergen information can lead to a recall or other action.
groups.low: An allergen is a substance in food that can trigger an allergic reaction, which may become severe or life-threatening. Read the whole label to help choose food you can eat safely. EU Regulation 1169/2011, Annex II, names 14 groups: cereals with gluten; crustaceans; eggs; fish; peanuts; soybeans; milk; listed tree nuts; celery; mustard; sesame; sulphur dioxide and sulphites; lupin; and molluscs. Crustaceans include crab and shrimp. Molluscs include mussels and oysters. Sulphites must be declared above 10 mg/kg or 10 mg/L, measured as total SO2. Some forms have legal exemptions. Allergens on prepacked food normally stand out in the ingredients list. The US list has nine: milk, eggs, fish, crustacean shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soybeans, and sesame. FALCPA covered the first eight. The FASTER Act added sesame on January 1, 2023. On relevant FDA-regulated packs, look for the allergen's name in the ingredients or a Contains statement beside them. A label that lists casein must also identify milk. Casein is a milk protein, but not all foods that cause allergies are included in these official lists. Do not assume EU and US labels follow the same rules. May contain has a different purpose. It warns of possible cross-contact, which occurs when a food picks up an allergen during handling, although these precautionary warnings are voluntary in the US. They do not excuse poor cleaning or poor controls. The EU does not have one general rule saying any trace must carry that exact warning. Check the full label every time. Recipes and manufacturing processes may change, while food sold abroad may follow different labeling requirements. A missing allergen can lead to a recall and other action.
groups.source_review: FDA sesame and labeling information checked; EU Annex II reference retained with thresholds and exemptions; no universal trace-label mandate asserted.
groups.notes: Corrected exclusion of sesame and mandatory May contain claims. Original Mid/Low FK bounds overlap; preserve bounds without implying large per-topic register gap.

groups.high: Drug development uses progressively larger clinical studies to characterize safety, dose, pharmacokinetics, and therapeutic benefit. The FDA's broad description places Phase I at roughly 20–100 participants, Phase II at up to several hundred, and Phase III at about 300–3,000. These are illustrative ranges rather than legally fixed enrollment requirements; older summaries often cite 20–80, 100–300, and 1,000–3,000. Phase I primarily examines tolerability, dose, adverse effects, and how the body absorbs, distributes, metabolizes, and eliminates the drug. Participants may be healthy volunteers or patients, particularly in oncology. Starting doses use relevant nonclinical evidence, with escalation governed by safeguards rather than a universal requirement to identify a maximum tolerated dose. Phase II investigates preliminary efficacy in patients with the target condition while refining dose and continuing safety assessment. Phase III provides larger confirmatory evidence of benefit and adverse reactions, often against placebo or established care. Randomization, blinding, suitable endpoints, and representative recruitment strengthen inference where appropriate; not every study uses the same design. FDA oversight includes the Investigational New Drug framework in 21 CFR Part 312, with marketing applications addressed in Part 314. ICH E8(R1) emphasizes quality by design and scientifically justified studies. Ethical review, informed consent, reliable data, and Good Clinical Practice are essential throughout. Favorable Phase III results do not guarantee approval: regulators assess the overall benefit-risk balance. Trials can overlap or use adaptive designs, and postapproval studies continue safety surveillance.
groups.mid: A new drug is tested in stages to learn whether it helps and what harm it may cause. Phase I mainly checks safety, dose, and how the body handles the drug. It may include healthy people or patients, such as people with cancer. Phase II tests early signs that it works in people with the disease. It also helps choose a dose and checks safety. Phase III tests benefit and side effects in larger groups. It often compares the drug with a dummy treatment, called a placebo, or with usual care. FDA examples give about 20–100 people for Phase I, up to several hundred for Phase II, and 300–3,000 for Phase III. These are rough ranges, not fixed legal rules. Older guides may say 20–80, 100–300, and 1,000–3,000. Before the trials, a sponsor uses the FDA Investigational New Drug process. This is part of 21 CFR Part 312. Part 314 covers drug marketing applications. ICH E8(R1) explains how to plan sound studies. Early doses use animal and other nonclinical evidence. Staff raise doses only under safety rules. Finding the highest tolerated dose is not the aim of every trial. A fair design may assign people by chance and hide who gets which treatment. It needs a clear way to measure the result. All stages need ethics review, informed consent, good records, and Good Clinical Practice. A drug can pass Phase III and still not be approved if its harms outweigh its benefits. Stages can overlap, and designs may change under planned rules. Safety checks also continue after approval.
groups.low: A new drug needs tests in people. These tests are called clinical trials. The stages answer different questions, with Phase I mainly checking safety and dose. It also checks what the body does with the drug. Some trials use healthy people. Others use patients, such as people with cancer. Phase II asks if the drug seems to help people with the disease. It checks doses and side effects too. Phase III tests more people. It looks for stronger proof of benefit and harm. The new drug may be compared with usual care. Or it may be compared with a dummy treatment called a placebo. FDA examples use about 20–100 people in Phase I. Phase II can use up to several hundred. Phase III may use 300–3,000. These are guides, not fixed rules. Older guides may use 20–80, 100–300, and 1,000–3,000. The sponsor uses the FDA's Investigational New Drug process before trials. The rules are in 21 CFR Part 312. Part 314 deals with requests to sell drugs. ICH E8(R1) guides sound study plans. Early doses use tests done before human trials. Any increase in dose must follow the study's safety rules and checks. Not every study seeks the highest dose a person can bear. People may be put into groups by chance. They may not know which treatment they get. Each study needs clear results to check. It also needs ethics review, informed consent, good records, and Good Clinical Practice. Good Phase III results do not promise approval. Benefits must outweigh harms. Stages can overlap. Checks for harm go on after a drug is approved.
groups.source_review: FDA clinical phase descriptions and sample ranges checked. Regulatory references are contextual, not a universal mandatory sequence or enrollment rule.
groups.notes: Removed incorrect 312.30 as initial IND rule, universal maximum tolerated/effective dose claims and fixed enrollment mandates.

groups.high: Adverse-event reporting supports pharmacovigilance by identifying harms that small or short clinical trials may miss. An adverse event is an unfavorable medical occurrence after exposure; it does not itself establish drug causation. An adverse reaction implies at least a suspected causal relationship. Seriousness is a regulatory category, distinct from symptom intensity: death, a life-threatening event, hospitalization or its prolongation, significant persistent disability, congenital anomaly, and other medically important events can qualify. Under ICH E2A's clinical-development framework, the sponsor expedites serious, unexpected suspected adverse reactions. Fatal or life-threatening qualifying cases require initial notification as soon as possible and no later than seven calendar days after the sponsor first knows the case qualifies, with fuller information within eight additional days. Other qualifying serious unexpected reactions require reporting within 15 calendar days of first sponsor knowledge. Do not wait for definitive causality or a complete investigation before an initial report. Investigators normally report serious events promptly to the sponsor according to the protocol and governing rules. These are not universal 7-day and 15-day deadlines for every healthcare professional or all postmarketing events. EU EudraVigilance receives relevant safety reports, but clinical-trial and postauthorization obligations differ. A useful case includes an identifiable patient and reporter, the suspected medicine, the reaction, timing, treatment, and outcome, with follow-up where needed. Reporting helps detect safety signals, reassess benefit-risk, and support warnings or regulatory action. Urgent clinical care must not wait for paperwork.
groups.mid: Reports of possible drug harm help find risks that trials may miss. An adverse event is a medical problem after someone uses a drug. It does not prove the drug caused it. An adverse reaction means a link is at least suspected. Serious does not just mean painful or severe. It can mean death, danger to life, a hospital stay, lasting disability, a birth defect, or another medically important event. ICH E2A sets rules for urgent reports during drug development. The trial sponsor reports serious, unexpected suspected reactions. For a fatal or life-threatening case, the sponsor must report as soon as possible, within seven calendar days of first knowing it qualifies. A fuller report follows within eight more days. Other serious unexpected suspected reactions must be reported within 15 calendar days of first sponsor knowledge. Do not wait to prove the cause or finish every test before sending the first report. Trial staff usually tell the sponsor promptly under the study's rules. These deadlines are not one general rule for every health worker or every problem after a drug goes on sale. EU EudraVigilance receives safety reports, but trial rules and postapproval rules differ. A useful report identifies the patient and reporter. It names the suspected drug and problem, when each occurred, what care was given, and the outcome. Send further details when they become known. Reports help experts find patterns, review benefits and harms, and decide if warnings or other action are needed. Give urgent care first; do not delay treatment to fill in a report.
groups.low: A drug can cause harm that early tests did not find, so reports help identify risks that need further investigation. An adverse event is a health problem after a drug is used. That alone does not prove the drug caused it. An adverse reaction means that a causal link between the medicine and the health problem is suspected. Serious has a special meaning here. It includes death, risk to life, a hospital stay, lasting harm, or a birth defect. Other medically important problems can count too. ICH E2A gives rules for urgent reports in drug trials. The sponsor runs or funds the trial. It must report serious, unexpected reactions that may be due to the drug. A fatal or life-threatening case needs a report as soon as possible. The limit is seven calendar days from when the sponsor first knows the case meets the rule. More details must follow within eight more days. For other cases that meet the rule, the limit is 15 calendar days. Staff must not delay the initial report while waiting for full proof of the cause or for every test to finish. Trial staff tell the sponsor promptly under the trial rules. These are not the same deadlines for all health workers or all drugs on sale. EU EudraVigilance takes safety reports. Clinical trial reporting requirements differ from the rules that apply after marketing authorization. A report needs a patient and a reporter who can be identified. Name the drug and the problem. Give dates, care given, and the outcome. Add new facts later. Experts use reports to look for patterns and decide on warnings or other action. If someone needs urgent care, get care first. Do not wait for the forms.
groups.source_review: ICH E2A expedited reporting definition and 7+8/15-day sponsor deadlines checked; EU trial reporting distinguished from postmarketing rules.
groups.notes: Corrected blanket healthcare-professional/postmarketing deadlines and requirement to establish causality before reporting.

groups.high: Cold-chain management limits microbial growth in perishable foods during storage, transport, and distribution. WHO's Five Keys to Safer Food advises prompt refrigeration, preferably below 5°C, and hot holding above 60°C. The intervening range is commonly described as the danger zone because many foodborne organisms can multiply rapidly there. The appropriate legal limit depends on the food, jurisdiction, and validated process; not every commodity has a universal mandatory 5°C limit. Some bacteria can double in approximately 20 minutes under favorable conditions, but that is not a fixed growth rate across the entire 5–60°C range. Growth depends on species, initial contamination, time, acidity, moisture, and other conditions. Refrigeration slows growth rather than sterilizing food; some organisms can still grow slowly when chilled. Some microbial toxins resist ordinary reheating, so cooking is not a reliable rescue for food stored unsafely. Monitor temperatures and minimize time outside controlled conditions. WHO advises against leaving cooked food at room temperature for more than two hours and recommends prompt refrigeration. Use an appropriate thermometer and follow product-specific storage instructions, including frozen-storage requirements where applicable. A brief temperature excursion is not automatically equivalent to a lethal contamination level, but it requires an assessment of time, temperature, and product risk. Codex General Principles of Food Hygiene, CXC 1-1969, supports hazard-based controls rather than an invented universal requirement for real-time telemetry. Temperature control complements clean handling, separation of raw and cooked food, and adequate cooking.
groups.mid: Cold-chain management keeps perishable food under controlled temperatures throughout storage, transport, and distribution. WHO's Five Keys to Safer Food says to chill food promptly, preferably below 5°C. Keep hot food above 60°C. Many harmful germs grow fast in the range between them, often called the danger zone. The precise legal temperature limit depends on the type of food, the validated process, and the relevant jurisdiction. There is not one 5°C law for every product. Some bacteria can double in about 20 minutes in ideal conditions. They do not all grow at that speed at every point from 5°C to 60°C. Growth also depends on the germ, time, moisture, acidity, and how much contamination was there at the start. Refrigeration slows microbial growth rather than sterilizing the food or eliminating every harmful organism. Some germs can still grow slowly in a fridge. Some toxins survive normal reheating, so cooking cannot always make badly stored food safe. Check temperatures with a suitable thermometer. Keep time outside safe storage as short as possible. WHO says not to leave cooked food at room temperature for more than two hours. Chill it promptly and follow the pack's storage rules. Frozen food needs its own storage limits. A brief rise in temperature does not prove the food is lethal. Assess how warm it got, for how long, and what food it was. Codex CXC 1-1969 calls for controls based on the hazards. It does not require every food business to use live digital tracking. Cold storage works with clean hands and tools, separate raw and cooked foods, and proper cooking.
groups.low: Keep food cold if it can spoil. The cold chain means keeping it cold as it moves from place to place. WHO recommends prompt refrigeration, preferably below 5°C, while hot food should stay above 60°C. Between 5°C and 60°C, many germs grow fast. This is called the danger zone. The legal storage limit can differ by food and place, so not all foods have one set 5°C rule. Some germs can double in about 20 minutes. That needs the right conditions. It is not true for all germs at all points in this range. Time, water, acid, and the number of germs at the start all matter. Refrigeration slows the growth of germs but does not destroy all of them. Some can still grow in the cold. Some germs make toxins. Normal heat may not destroy those toxins. Do not rely on cooking to save food kept the wrong way. Check food with a thermometer. Keep time out of the cold short. WHO says not to leave cooked food out for more than two hours. Chill it soon. Read the pack for storage rules. Frozen food has its own needs. A short rise in heat does not prove food will kill you. Check the food, how warm it got, and how long it stayed warm. Codex CXC 1-1969 calls for checks that suit the risk. It does not say all firms need live digital tracking. Keep hands and tools clean too. Keep raw food apart from cooked food. Cook food well.
groups.source_review: WHO safe-temperature and two-hour advice checked; avoided false universal kinetic or legal claims.
groups.notes: Removed universal mandatory <=5°C, automatic lethal excursion, fixed 10^8 CFU/g and universal real-time telemetry claims.

groups.high: An exclusion zone restricts access or residence where contamination or projected radiation dose makes ordinary use unsafe. It is not automatically a 30 km circle following an INES Level 7 accident. INES communicates event severity; Level 7 denotes a major accident, not a prescribed evacuation distance. Chernobyl's 1986 response included a roughly 30 km exclusion zone. At Fukushima Daiichi in 2011, evacuation expanded to 20 km; people 20–30 km away were initially advised to shelter, followed by further protective measures and location-specific restrictions. Those histories are not interchangeable. IAEA GSR Part 7, Preparedness and Response for a Nuclear or Radiological Emergency, establishes emergency-preparedness and response requirements. It is not the International Basic Safety Standards, which are GSR Part 3. Protective decisions depend on the release, projected dose, weather, contamination measurements, routes of exposure, and practical evacuation risks. Emergency evacuation and sheltering address immediate exposure, whereas longer-term relocation or access controls address persistent contamination. Boundaries may be irregular, may extend beyond an initial radius, and need reassessment as monitoring and remediation progress. Restricted areas require authorization, exposure controls, monitoring, and management of contaminated material. A place outside a marked circle is not automatically safe, and a low reading at one location does not authorize re-entry. Follow official instructions on evacuation routes, sheltering, food and water, and return. Longer-term restrictions can persist for years, but their duration is determined by assessed conditions and protective policy, not the INES label alone.
groups.mid: An exclusion zone is an area where entry or living is restricted because of radiation risk. It is not always a circle 30 km wide from the plant. INES Level 7 means a major nuclear accident. It describes how serious the event is; it does not set one evacuation distance. Chernobyl in 1986 had a zone of about 30 km. At Fukushima Daiichi in 2011, people within 20 km were evacuated. Those 20–30 km away were first told to stay indoors. Later steps and local restrictions changed with the conditions. These were not the same rules for two places. IAEA GSR Part 7 gives emergency planning and response rules. The International Basic Safety Standards is a different document, GSR Part 3. Officials assess what was released, expected dose, wind, rain, contamination, and how people could be exposed. They also weigh the risks of moving people. Leaving an area or sheltering can cut immediate exposure. Longer-term limits on living or entry deal with contamination that remains. The boundary need not be round. Unsafe places can lie beyond the first zone. Monitoring and cleanup can change the boundary over time. Entry needs permission and controls to limit exposure. Teams also manage contaminated waste. Do not assume that outside a circle means safe. One low reading does not give permission to return. Follow official advice on routes, shelter, food, water, and re-entry. Restrictions can last years, but their length depends on measured conditions and protective policy, not just an INES score.
groups.low: An exclusion zone is a place you may not enter or live in without permission. Radiation may make it unsafe. It is not always a 30 km circle. INES Level 7 means a major nuclear accident. That score does not tell you how far to move. At Chernobyl in 1986, the zone was about 30 km. At Fukushima Daiichi in 2011, people within 20 km had to leave. Those 20–30 km away were first told to stay inside. More steps followed as the risks became clear. The two emergencies required different protective measures because their releases and local conditions differed. IAEA GSR Part 7 is a guide for emergency plans and response. GSR Part 3 is a different set of safety standards. Officials check the release, dose, wind, rain, and dirt or water with radioactive material in it. They check how people could be exposed. They also check the risk of moving people. Leaving or staying inside can cut the first exposure. Limits on living in a place can last much longer. A zone may have an uneven shape. Some places beyond it may still be unsafe. Tests and cleanup can lead to changes. Entry needs permission and safety checks. Waste must be managed too. Outside the circle does not mean safe. One low test result does not mean you can return. Follow official advice on where to go, where to stay, and what to eat or drink. Limits may last years. Their length depends on the actual risk, not just the INES score.
groups.source_review: IAEA Fukushima report distinguishes20 km evacuation/20–30 km shelter; checked GSR Part7 title and non-universal response framing.
groups.notes: Corrected universal30 km Level7 protocol, Fukushima history and GSR Part7 misidentification.

groups.high: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.146 governs permit-required confined spaces in its applicable workplaces. A confined space permits bodily entry, has restricted entry or exit, and is not designed for continuous occupancy. A permit space has an actual or potential hazardous atmosphere, engulfment risk, a trapping or asphyxiating configuration, or another recognized serious hazard. Oxygen below 19.5% is deficient; above 23.5% is enriched. Readings within that range do not alone establish safe entry: flammable or toxic contaminants and physical hazards must also be controlled. Oxygen depletion can impair judgment, produce collapse, and rapidly kill; effects depend on concentration, pressure, exposure, and the individual, so fixed 16% and 6% symptom rules must not replace assessment. Test with suitable calibrated equipment before entry: oxygen first, combustible gases and vapors second, toxic gases and vapors third. Record acceptable conditions and monitor as necessary to ensure they continue; OSHA does not impose a universal 15-minute retest interval for every ventilated space. Isolate energy and material inflows, control hazards, use ventilation where appropriate, and implement the applicable written entry-permit system, trained roles, communications, and rescue arrangements. Limited alternative procedures or reclassification require the standard's conditions, not merely a favorable oxygen reading. An outside attendant and suitable retrieval or rescue capability are crucial under the permit program. Never enter impulsively to rescue a collapsed worker: an unprotected rescuer can become another casualty. Leave immediately if unsafe conditions arise and follow the established emergency plan.
groups.mid: A confined space is large enough to enter but hard to get in or out of. It is not meant for people to work in all the time. OSHA 29 CFR 1910.146 requires permits for covered spaces with serious hazards. These can include bad air, material that can bury you, a shape that can trap you, or other major risks. Oxygen below 19.5% is too low. Above 23.5% it increases fire risk. A reading in between does not prove the space is safe. Poisonous or flammable gas can still be there. Low oxygen can cause poor judgment, collapse, or death. Do not use 16% or 6% as a safe line to test your limits. Effects vary. Trained staff test with suitable calibrated equipment before entry. They check oxygen first, gases that can burn second, and toxic gases third. They record the safe entry conditions. They keep testing or monitoring as needed during the work. There is no general rule to test only every 15 minutes when a fan is running. Shut off and isolate energy and material flows. Control other hazards and use suitable ventilation. Follow the written permit rules, with trained people, contact with an outside attendant, and a rescue plan. Some special exceptions exist, but a good oxygen reading alone does not qualify a space. Have the right rescue or retrieval kit ready. If someone collapses inside, do not rush in unprotected. The same air can kill you too. Leave if conditions become unsafe and use the emergency plan.
groups.low: A tank or pit can be hard to get out of. It may be a confined space. It is not built for people to stay in. OSHA 29 CFR 1910.146 sets rules for many such spaces at work. A permit is needed if a covered space has serious risks. Bad air can kill. Loose material can bury you. The shape can trap you. Other hazards count too. Oxygen below 19.5% is too low. Above 23.5% there is more fire risk. A reading in between is not proof of safety. The air may still have gas that burns or poisons you. Too little oxygen can make you confused. You may fall and die. Do not treat 16% or 6% as a safe test of what you can bear. Effects vary. Trained staff must test the air before entry. Use a suitable, calibrated instrument that has been checked to give reliable readings for the hazards present. Test oxygen first. Then test gases that burn. Test toxic gases last. Record the safe entry conditions. Keep testing or monitoring as needed to ensure that acceptable entry conditions continue throughout the work. A fan does not mean a test every 15 minutes is enough. Block off energy and flows of material. Deal with other risks. Use safe air flow where needed. Follow the permit plan. Have trained staff, an attendant outside, a way to keep in touch, and a rescue plan. A good oxygen test alone does not waive these rules. If someone falls inside, do not rush in. You could die too. Leave if the space becomes unsafe. Use the trained rescue team and suitable retrieval equipment set out in the emergency plan.
groups.source_review: OSHA permit-space criteria, oxygen cutoffs, testing order and monitoring duties checked.
groups.notes: Corrected reversed test order and false universal15-minute rule; removed physiological threshold guarantees and oxygen-only safety claim.

groups.high: Lockout/tagout controls hazardous energy during machinery servicing and maintenance. OSHA 29 CFR 1910.147 requires an applicable energy-control program, employee training, procedures, and periodic inspections. Hazards include electrical supply, hydraulic or pneumatic pressure, gravity, heat, and stored mechanical or chemical energy. A stop button is not an energy-isolating device. An authorized employee first identifies the energy sources, hazards, and isolation methods, informs affected workers, and shuts down the machine in an orderly manner. All relevant energy-isolating devices are operated and secured with the prescribed personal lockout or permitted tagout devices. Stored energy must then be relieved, disconnected, restrained, or otherwise made safe. Before work, the employee verifies isolation and de-energization using appropriate tests; an unsuccessful start attempt alone may not prove absence of every hazard. Reaccumulating energy requires continuing checks. When equipment can be locked out, lockout is generally required unless a tagout system provides the equivalent protection specified by the standard. A warning tag alone is not a physical restraint. Group work and shift changes need procedures preserving each worker's protection. Before restoration, inspect the equipment, clear or position workers safely, and notify affected employees. Devices are normally removed by the employee who applied them; exceptional employer-directed removal requires the standard's safeguards. The standard distinguishes authorized employees who perform servicing from affected workers who use or work near the equipment. Certain work, such as exclusively controlled unplugged cord-and-plug equipment, has defined exceptions. Do not substitute an unsupported injury percentage for the actual prevention requirements.
groups.mid: Lockout/tagout, or LOTO, stops a machine from starting or releasing stored energy while people service it. OSHA 29 CFR 1910.147 requires a safety program, staff training, work steps, and regular checks. Energy may be electric power, air or fluid pressure, heat, weight, springs, or chemicals. A stop button is not enough. First, a trained authorized worker finds all energy sources and how to isolate them. Tell affected workers, then stop the machine in the normal safe way. Isolate each source and use the required personal locks or allowed tags. Release trapped pressure and other stored energy. Block or secure parts that could move or fall. Before work starts, test that all energy is safely controlled. Trying the start button alone may miss some risks. Keep checking if energy could build up again. Use locks where the device can be locked, unless a tag system meets OSHA's equal-protection rules. A tag warns people; it does not hold a switch or valve shut. Group jobs and shift changes need a plan so each worker stays protected. Before power returns, check the machine, get workers clear or safely placed, and tell affected staff. The person who put on a lock or tag normally removes it. Other removal needs special safeguards. Authorized workers do the service and energy control. Affected workers use the machine or work near it. Some limited exceptions exist, such as a tool unplugged with its plug under the service worker's sole control. Do not rely on a guessed injury rate instead of these steps.
groups.low: LOTO means lockout/tagout. It keeps a machine off while work is done on it. It also stops trapped energy from hurting you. The US rule is OSHA 29 CFR 1910.147. The boss needs a plan, training, work steps, and checks. Electrical power is not the only source of hazardous energy. Air, oil, heat, springs, weight, and chemicals can hurt you too. A stop button is not enough. A trained worker must find each source. Tell those who use the machine. Stop it in a safe way. Cut off each source. Put the right personal lock or allowed tag on it. Let trapped pressure out. Block parts that could move or fall. Test that the machine has no unsafe energy before work. Just trying to start it may not check all risks. Check again if energy can build up. Use a lock if the device can be locked. A tag alone needs the extra protection the rule calls for. A tag warns you. It does not hold a valve shut. A team job needs a plan to keep each worker safe. So does a shift change. Before restart, check the machine. Get people clear or safe. Tell those who work near it. Each worker should remove their own lock or tag. Someone else may do so only under special safeguards. Some jobs have narrow exceptions. One is a tool with its plug out and in the worker's sole control. Do not skip the plan based on a guessed injury rate.

groups.high: The UN Globally Harmonized System of Classification and Labelling of Chemicals (GHS) provides hazard-classification criteria and standardized communication. Revision 10 is the dataset's 2023 reference edition, not a claim that every jurisdiction currently implements that edition. GHS itself is not a universally binding law; national systems adopt selected provisions on different schedules. Chemical labels commonly include product and supplier identification, appropriate pictograms, a signal word, hazard statements, and precautionary statements. Danger denotes more severe categories than Warning where those words apply. A flame indicates relevant fire hazards; a skull and crossbones indicates specified acute-toxicity categories. A Safety Data Sheet (SDS) communicates more detailed information using 16 sections: 1 identification; 2 hazard identification; 3 composition/ingredients; 4 first aid; 5 firefighting; 6 accidental release; 7 handling/storage; 8 exposure controls/personal protection; 9 physical/chemical properties; 10 stability/reactivity; 11 toxicology; 12 ecology; 13 disposal; 14 transport; 15 regulatory information; and 16 other information, including preparation or revision. Section 2, rather than Section 1, contains the principal label-hazard information. Ingredient disclosure thresholds and exceptions vary by hazard and jurisdiction; there is no universal 1% rule for every ingredient. Consult the relevant SDS for exposure limits, suitable gloves or respirators, spill control, incompatible materials, and emergency actions. Keep labels and SDS information current under applicable national deadlines and accessible in a language workers understand. US OSHA's Hazard Communication Standard and EU CLP/REACH implement related but nonidentical requirements; OSHA does not enforce SDS sections 12–15's substantive content. An SDS supports training and controls but does not itself make a chemical safe.
groups.mid: GHS is the UN system for naming chemical hazards and giving clear warnings. This dataset uses Revision 10 from 2023. That does not mean every country uses the same edition or rules. GHS is a model; each place makes its own law. A label usually gives the product and supplier names, warning pictures, a signal word, hazard statements, and safe-use advice. Danger marks more severe hazards than Warning where these words apply. A flame marks certain fire risks. A skull and crossbones marks certain acute poisoning risks. The Safety Data Sheet, or SDS, gives more detail in 16 sections. Section 1 identifies the product and supplier. Section 2 gives hazards and label information. Section 3 lists ingredients. Sections 4, 5, and 6 cover first aid, firefighting, and spills. Sections 7 and 8 cover safe handling and storage, exposure controls, and protective kit. Section 9 gives physical and chemical properties. Section 10 explains stability and reactions. Section 11 covers health effects. Sections 12, 13, and 14 cover effects on nature, disposal, and transport. Section 15 gives legal information. Section 16 gives other details and dates of updates. There is no single 1% rule for listing all ingredients; the hazard and local law matter. Read the SDS for safe limits, gloves, breathing protection, spills, and substances that must be kept apart. Keep it up to date under local deadlines and in a language staff understand. US OSHA and EU CLP/REACH rules differ. OSHA does not enforce the content requirements of sections 12–15. A sheet is not a substitute for training or controls.
groups.low: GHS is a UN system for chemical hazard warnings. This dataset uses Revision 10, from 2023. Not all places use that version. Each country makes its own rules. GHS is not one law for the whole world. Read the label before you use a chemical. It usually names the product and supplier. It shows warning pictures, words, hazards, and safe-use steps. Danger means a more severe hazard than Warning where those words apply. A flame can warn of fire. A skull and crossbones can warn of acute poisoning. Read the Safety Data Sheet too. It is called an SDS. It has 16 sections. Section 1 names the product and supplier. Section 2 gives hazards and label warnings. Section 3 lists ingredients. Section 4 gives first aid. Section 5 deals with fire. Section 6 deals with spills. Section 7 covers use and storage. Section 8 gives exposure controls and protective kit. Section 9 gives the chemical's properties. Section 10 explains what can react or change. Section 11 gives health effects. Section 12 covers harm to nature. Section 13 covers waste. Section 14 covers transport. Section 15 gives legal details. Section 16 has other facts and update dates. There is no one 1% rule for all ingredients. The hazard and local law matter. Look up safe limits, gloves, masks or respirators, spills, and things to keep apart. Keep the sheet current. Staff need it in a language they understand. US OSHA and EU CLP/REACH rules differ. OSHA does not enforce the content of sections 12–15. A sheet does not make a chemical safe. You still need training and controls.

groups.high: ICRP Publication 103 and the IAEA International Basic Safety Standards distinguish planned public exposure from occupational, medical, and emergency exposure. The public effective-dose limit is normally 1 mSv per year for regulated planned exposures. It is not a cap on all radiation a person receives. Patient medical exposure and ordinary natural background are excluded from this public limit, although some controllable natural-source activities have regulatory requirements. Medical exposures require clinical justification and optimization rather than an indiscriminate annual patient cap. Natural background varies substantially; the often-cited worldwide average is about 2.4 mSv per year. Adult occupational effective-dose limits under the international framework are 20 mSv per year averaged over five consecutive years, with no more than 50 mSv in any single year; national law may differ. In specially authorized circumstances, public exposure in one year may exceed 1 mSv only if the five-year average remains no greater than 1 mSv per year. This is not a general allowance for 15 mSv over five years. Effective dose combines organ doses with tissue-weighting factors to support protection planning; it is not an exact individualized prediction of cancer risk. The linear no-threshold model is a prudent basis for protection at low doses, not proof that every small exposure produces a measurable cancer case. Dose limits complement justification and optimization, including ALARA. Emergencies and persistent postaccident exposures use different protective reference levels and decisions; they do not authorize unlimited exposure. Keep routine releases below applicable limits and follow the responsible regulator's requirements.
groups.mid: Within the international radiation-protection framework, the public effective-dose limit is normally 1 mSv per year for regulated planned exposure. This comes from the ICRP and IAEA protection framework. It does not count every source of radiation in your life. Ordinary natural background and medical exposure as a patient are not included in this public limit. Some natural sources can still be regulated when an activity brings them under control. Doctors must justify scans and treatment and keep doses suitable for the medical purpose. A blanket yearly cap could prevent useful care. Natural background varies widely; its often-used world average is about 2.4 mSv per year. For adult radiation workers, the international effective-dose limit is 20 mSv per year averaged over five years, and no more than 50 mSv in any one year. National legislation may establish different occupational requirements, so the responsible regulator's rules must be checked. A regulator can allow a special higher public dose in one year only if the average over five years stays at or below 1 mSv per year. That is not permission for 15 mSv over five years. Effective dose combines doses to different organs using factors for their sensitivity. It helps plan protection, but it is not a precise personal cancer forecast. The linear no-threshold model assumes risk rises with dose for protection purposes. It does not prove that each tiny dose causes a measurable case of cancer. Limits work with justification and optimization: use radiation only when justified and keep exposure as low as reasonably achievable, or ALARA. Emergency and postaccident situations use different reference levels and protective choices. They do not mean there is no limit to risk or control. Follow your regulator's requirements.
groups.low: For planned, regulated exposure, the public dose limit is usually 1 mSv a year. ICRP and IAEA standards use this limit. It does not count radiation from every source in your life. Ordinary natural background radiation and medical exposure received as a patient are excluded from this public effective-dose limit. Some natural sources can still need controls when people use or manage them. A scan or treatment must have a sound medical reason. Its expected benefit should justify it, and the dose should fit the need. A fixed annual patient cap could block care that helps. Natural background differs by place. The often-used world average is about 2.4 mSv a year. Adult workers have a different international limit: an average of 20 mSv a year over five years. They must not get more than 50 mSv in one year. National regulations may use different limits or additional restrictions, so check the responsible regulator's requirements. A special public dose above 1 mSv in one year needs approval. The five-year average must still be no more than 1 mSv a year. It is not a 15 mSv allowance over five years. Effective dose combines doses to organs, with factors for how sensitive they are. This weighted measure supports radiation-protection planning, rather than providing a precise prediction of an individual's lifetime cancer risk. The linear no-threshold model is used to plan protection. It assumes added dose adds risk. It does not prove each tiny dose causes a cancer case that can be measured. Use radiation only for a justified purpose. Keep doses as low as reasonably achievable: ALARA. Emergency exposure and persistent contamination after an accident use different protective reference levels, but still require assessment and control. Follow the responsible regulator's rules.
